# Introduction

## Phase-type distributions

::: {.absolute top="25%"}
- **"Distribution of time to absorption of a discrete space Markov jump process."**
:::

::: {.absolute top="40%"}
- **Lots** of other applications
  - "What is the distribution of time water molecules spend in each tank of a sewage treatment plant?"
  - "How likely are all packets of data to reach a server in less than some time?"
  - "How much time do lineages of a coalescent or ARG spend spend in different states?"
:::

## Waiting time in the coalescent is\n**phase-type distributed**

::: {.absolute top="30%" left="0%" width="50%"}
![](./images/coal_mc_jump_anim_5.svg){.nostretch fig-align="left"}
:::

::: {.absolute top="25%" left="60%"}

$\tau \sim \mathrm{PH}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, {\color{blue} \boldsymbol{S}})$

$\boldsymbol{\alpha} = (1,\; 0, \; 0, \; 0)$

${\color{blue}\boldsymbol{S}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-6 &  6  &  & \\
   & -3  & 1  & 2 \\
   &     & -1  & \\
   &     &  & -1 \\
\end{bmatrix}$
:::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## **Moments** of a phase-type distribution

::: {.absolute top="25%" left="10%" .larger }
$$
\mathbb{E}[\tau] = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U} \mathbf{e} \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \boldsymbol{U} = -\boldsymbol{S}^{-1}
$$
:::

::: {.absolute top="50%" left="10%" .larger}
$$\mathbb{E}[\tau^k] = k! \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}^k \mathbf{e}$$
:::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## **CDF/PDF** for a phase-type distribution

::: {.absolute top="25%" left="10%" .larger }
$$F(t) = 1 - \boldsymbol{\alpha} e^{\boldsymbol{S}t} \mathbf{e}, \quad t \geq 0$$
:::

::: {.absolute top="50%" left="10%" .larger}
$$f(t) = \boldsymbol{\alpha} e^{\boldsymbol{S}t} (-\boldsymbol{S}) \mathbf{e}, \quad t \geq 0$$
:::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Marginal moments

::: {.absolute top="20%" }
$k$-th moment of the reward-transformed distribution:
:::

::: {.absolute top="30%" left="10%" .larger }
$$\mathbb{E}[Y^k] = k! \boldsymbol{\alpha} (\boldsymbol{U} \boldsymbol{\Delta}(\boldsymbol{r}))^k \mathbf{e}$$
:::

::: {.absolute top="50%" }
where $\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is a diagonal matrix with rewards on the diagonal.
:::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->

## Multivariate Phase-Type Distributions

**Multivariate phase-type distributions** assign a vector of rewards to each state, resulting in a vector-valued outcome:

$$\boldsymbol{Y} \sim MPH^*(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{S}, \boldsymbol{R})$$

where $\boldsymbol{R}$ is a matrix of rewards (each row corresponds to a state, each column to a reward dimension).

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Advantages of Graph Representation

Sparsely connected state spaces:

- **Memory efficiency**:
  - Store only existing transitions (not full $p \times p$ matrix)
- **Computational efficiency**: Operations on edges only
  - Many algorithms: $O(|V|^2)$ vs $O(p^3)$ for matrix operations
- **Iterative construction**: Build state space incrementally
  - Add vertices and edges as needed
  - Natural for complex phenomena
- **Intuitive modeling**: Specify transitions from each state independently
  - Markov property: next state depends only on current state
  - Easy to encode complex models

::: todo
- Big O notation for algorithms
:::


As var as the interaction between two adjacent epochs, it does not matter if the former epoch comprise multiple epoch or not. So for starters we just need to consider a two epoch model.

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Use case

```python
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-10|11-13"
#| output-location: column-fragment

from phasic import Graph

def coalescent(state):
    transitions = []
    for i in range(state.size):
        for j in range(i, state.size):            
            same = int(i == j)
            if same and state[i] < 2:
                continue
            if not same and (state[i] < 1 or state[j] < 1):
                continue 
            new = state.copy()
            new[i] -= 1
            new[j] -= 1
            new[i+j+1] += 1
            rate = state[i]*(state[j]-same)/(1+same)
            transitions.append((new, rate))
    return transitions

nr_samples = 4
initial_state = [nr_samples]+[0]*(nr_samples-1)
graph = Graph(coalescent, ipv=initial_state)
#graph.plot()
graph.expectation()

```

# DAG construction
<!-- =============================================================================== -->
<!-- =============================================================================== -->

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## DAG construction

Constructing an **acyclic graph** retaining the expected accumulated rewards

Turns out this is Gaussian elimination on the graph - in effect solving a linear system.

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Rate **standardization**

![](./images/normalization.svg)

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Constructing an **acyclic graph**

![](./images/elimination1.svg){.nostretch width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::::: {layout="[-0.05,0.4,-0.05,0.4]"}
::: column
**Edges:**<br>

$w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{D}) = w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{A})\, w(\mathrm{A}\rightarrow \mathrm{D})$

**Vertices:**<br>

$x_A \leftarrow x_C + x_A$
:::

::: column
Insert the first equation in the third:<br>

$\begin{align*}
T_C &= 5 + (5 + 0.6 \cdot T_B + 0.4 \cdot T_D) \\
&= 10 + 0.6 \cdot T_B + 0.4 \cdot T_D
\end{align*}$
:::
:::::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Constructing an **acyclic graph**

![](./images/elimination2.svg){.nostretch width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::::: {layout="[-0.1,0.4,-0.05,0.4]"}
::: column
$x_\mathrm{C} +\!\,= x_\mathrm{A}\, w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{A})$

$x_C \leftarrow 0.6 \cdot x_C$
:::

::: column
Insert the second equation in the third:<br>

$\begin{align*}
T_C &= 5 + T_A + 0.6 \cdot ( T_B + 0.5 \cdot T_C + 0.5 \cdot T_D) \\
&= 11.2 + 0.3 \cdot T_C + 0.7 \cdot T_D
\end{align*}$
:::
:::::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Constructing an **acyclic graph**

![](./images/elimination3.svg){.nostretch width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::::: {layout="[-0.1,0.4,-0.05,0.4]"}
::: column
$x_C \leftarrow x_C + x_C \cdot \big(\frac{1}{1-0.6}-1\big)$
:::

::: column
Isolate $T_C$ in the third equation to remove self-loop:<br>

$\begin{align*}
T_C &= 11.2 + 0.3 \cdot T_C + 0.7 \cdot T_C \\
&= 16 + T_D
\end{align*}$
:::
:::::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Constructing an **acyclic graph**

![](./images/elimination4.svg){.nostretch width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::::: {layout="[-0.1,0.4,-0.05,0.4]"}
::: column
:::

::: column
:::
:::::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Constructing an **acyclic graph**

![](./images/elimination5.svg){.nostretch width="80%" fig-align="center"}

::::: {layout="[-0.1,0.4,-0.05,0.4]"}
::: column
:::

::: column
:::

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Constructing an **acyclic graph** retaining the expected accumulated rewards

:::::: {layout="[0.24,-0.05,0.4,-0.05,0.25]"}
::: column
$\begin{align*}
T_A &= 5 + 0.6 \cdot T_B + 0.4 \cdot T_D \\
T_B &= 2 + 0.5 \cdot T_C + 0.5 \cdot T_D \\
T_C &= 5 + T_A \\
T_D &= 0
\end{align*}$

Insert the first equation in the third:\
$\begin{align*}
T_C &= 5 + (5 + 0.6 \cdot T_B + 0.4 \cdot T_D) \\
&= 10 + 0.6 \cdot T_B + 0.4 \cdot T_D
\end{align*}$

Insert the second equation in the third:\
$\begin{align*}
T_C &= 5 + T_A + 0.6 \cdot ( T_B + 0.5 \cdot T_C + 0.5 \cdot T_D) \\
&= 11.2 + 0.3 \cdot T_C + 0.7 \cdot T_D
\end{align*}$

Isolate $T_C$ in the third equation to remove self-loop:\
$\begin{align*}
T_C &= 11.2 + 0.3 \cdot T_C + 0.7 \cdot T_C \\
&= 16 + T_D
\end{align*}$

The equations are now:\
$\begin{align*}
T_A &= 5 + 0.6 \cdot T_B + 0.4 \cdot T_D \\
T_B &= 2 + 0.5 \cdot T_C + T_D\\
T_C &= 16 + T_D \\
T_D &= 16
\end{align*}$
:::

::: column
:::

::: column
$$w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{D}) = w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{A})\, w(\mathrm{A}\rightarrow \mathrm{D})$$

$$x_\mathrm{C} +\!\,= x_\mathrm{A}\, w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{A})$$

$$w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{D}) = \frac{w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{D})}{1 - w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{C})}$$

$$x_\mathrm{C} +\!\,= x_\mathrm{C} \left ( \frac{1}{1-w(\mathrm{C}\rightarrow \mathrm{C})} - 1\right)$$
:::
::::::

# Discrete Phase-Type Distributions
<!-- =============================================================================== -->
<!-- =============================================================================== -->

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Discrete Phase-Type Distributions

For discrete phase-type distributions with sub-transition matrix $\boldsymbol{T}$ and initial distribution $\boldsymbol{\pi}$:

Green Matrix

$$\boldsymbol{U} = -(\boldsymbol{T} - \boldsymbol{I})^{-1}$$

CDF (Probability Mass Function)

The probability of absorption at exactly jump $t$:

$$F(t) = 1 - \boldsymbol{\pi} \boldsymbol{T}^t \mathbf{e}$$

Moments

The expectation:

$$\mathbb{E}[\tau] = \boldsymbol{\pi} \boldsymbol{U} \mathbf{e}$$

# Higher-order moments
<!-- =============================================================================== -->
<!-- =============================================================================== -->

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Higher-order **moments**

![](./images/moment_computation_example.svg)

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## The variance

$$\text{Var}(\tau) = 2\boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}^2 \mathbf{e} - (\boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U} \mathbf{e})^2$$

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Higher-order **moments**

k’th moment: $\mathbb{E}[\tau^k]=k!\boldsymbol{\alpha} (\boldsymbol{U}\triangle(\boldsymbol{r}))^{k}\mathbf{e}$

Expectation: $\mathbb{E}[\tau] = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}\triangle(\boldsymbol{r})\mathbf{e}$

2'nd moment: $\mathbb{E}[\tau^2] = 2\cdot\boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}\triangle(\boldsymbol{r})\boldsymbol{U}\triangle(\boldsymbol{r})\mathbf{e}$

$\mathbb{E}[\tau] = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}\! \triangle\!\,(\boldsymbol{r}) \mathbf{e} = \boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}  \mathbf{e}$ (assuming unit rewards for simplicity).

$\mathbb{E}[\tau^2] = 2\cdot\boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{U}\mathbf{e}$

$\boldsymbol{U}\mathbf{e} = \boldsymbol{r'} = \triangle\!\,(\boldsymbol{r'}) \mathbf{e}$. So the variance can be written as: $\mathbb{E}[\tau^2] = 2\cdot\boldsymbol{\alpha} \boldsymbol{U}\!\triangle\!\,(\boldsymbol{r'}) \mathbf{e}$, where $\boldsymbol{r'}$ are the waiting times computed for the first moment.

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Higher-order **moments**

- Higher-order moments are the expectation with different rewards.
- Keep a parameterized list of graph manipulations to avoid redoing the O(V3) expensive conversion to acyclic.
- Rewards are applied as scalars and do not require recomputation.
- Additional moments can then be computed in O(V2) time.

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Higher-order **moments**

**1’ moment: 3**

![](./images/first-moment.svg){.nostretch width="50%" fig-align="left"}

`expected_waiting_time(graph)` → $(\boldsymbol{3},\ 3,\ 2,\ 1,\ 0)$

**2’ moment: 12**

![](./images/second-moment.svg){.nostretch width="50%" fig-align="left"}

`expected_waiting_time(graph, expected_waiting_time(graph))` → $(\boldsymbol{6},\ 6,\ 3,\ 1,\ 0)$

<!-- =============================================================================== -->
## Joint moments

The covariance between dimensions $i$ and $j$:

$$\text{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j) = \boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{R}_{\cdot i})\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{R}_{\cdot j})\mathbf{e} + \boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{R}_{\cdot j})\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{R}_{\cdot i})\mathbf{e} - \boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{R}_{\cdot i})\mathbf{e} \cdot \boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{R}_{\cdot j})\mathbf{e}$$

## Practical Example

Let's compute properties of an Erlang distribution (sum of exponential random variables):

``` python
from phasic import Graph

# Build Erlang(3) distribution: sum of 3 exponentials with rate 1
g = Graph(1)
start = g.starting_vertex()

# Create chain: S -> v1 -> v2 -> v3 -> absorbing
v1 = g.find_or_create_vertex([1])
v2 = g.find_or_create_vertex([2])
v3 = g.find_or_create_vertex([3])

start.add_edge(v1, 1.0)  # Start in state 1 with probability 1
v1.add_edge(v2, 1.0)     # Transition rate 1
v2.add_edge(v3, 1.0)     # Transition rate 1
v3.add_edge(g.find_or_create_vertex([4]), 1.0)  # To absorbing state

# Compute properties
print(f"Expectation: {g.expectation()}")      # Should be 3.0
print(f"Variance: {g.variance()}")            # Should be 3.0
print(f"PDF at t=2.0: {g.pdf(2.0)}")
print(f"CDF at t=2.0: {g.cdf(2.0)}")
```

## Further Reading

For detailed algorithms and proofs, see:

**Røikjer, T., Hobolth, A., & Munch, K. (2022).** *Graph-based algorithms for phase-type distributions.* Statistics and Computing, 32:103. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-022-10174-3>

The paper provides: - Complete algorithmic details - Complexity analysis - Proofs of correctness - Empirical performance comparisons - Applications to population genetics
